steps.prompt: A cone and a cylinder have the same base and the same height. How many cones of water do you think it takes to fill the cylinder?

cards.title: Volume and surface
cards.body: Box: $V = abc$, surface $2(ab + bc + ca)$. Prism or cylinder: base area $\times$ height, so a cylinder is $\pi r^2 h$ with curved area $2\pi r h$. Pyramid or cone: $\frac{1}{3}$ base area $\times$ height; a cone's curved area is $\pi r \ell$, where $\ell$ is the slant height. Sphere: $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, surface $4\pi r^2$.

cards.title: Worked example: a cylinder
cards.problem: A cylinder has radius $3$ and height $5$. What is its volume?

try.prompt: What is the area of the base? Write it with π.

cards.title: Scaling and cubes
cards.body: Multiply every length by $k$: areas multiply by $k^2$ and volumes by $k^3$. A painted $n \times n \times n$ cube cut into unit cubes has $8$ corner cubes (3 painted faces), $12(n - 2)$ edge cubes (2 faces), $6(n - 2)^2$ face cubes (1 face) and $(n - 2)^3$ unpainted cubes.

cards.title: Worked example: a painted cube
cards.problem: A $4 \times 4 \times 4$ cube is painted and cut into unit cubes. How many have no paint? How many have paint on exactly one face?

steps.text: The inside cubes form a $2 \times 2 \times 2$ block: $8$.

try.prompt: How many have exactly one painted face?

cards.title: The common trap: forgetting the third
cards.body: Cones and pyramids are a THIRD of the matching cylinder or prism. Use the radius, not the diameter. And keep area ($r^2$) and volume ($r^3$) formulas apart.

prompts: Which solid formula do you find hardest to remember, and how will you remember it?
